title: Algorithmic complexity
summary: Complexity describes how the amount of work grows as the input grows. It is not how long one run takes on your machine.

sections.heading: What it measures
sections.body: We count basic steps as a function of the input size `n`. Doubling `n` tells you more than a stopwatch: a single loop over a list does about twice the work for a list twice as long, while a loop inside a loop does about four times the work.

sections.heading: Shapes you will meet
sections.body:
`O(1)`: the same work however big the input is, like `xs[0]`.

`O(n)`: one pass over the data, like a single `for` loop over a list.

`O(n²)`: a pass inside a pass over the same data.

`O(log n)`: the problem is halved each step, like binary search in sorted data.

In Python, `x in some_list` is a pass over the list (`O(n)`), while `x in some_set` is about `O(1)` on average.

sections.heading: Why a nested loop is about n squared
sections.body: If the inner loop only looks at the items after the current one, it does (n - 1) + (n - 2) + ... + 1 comparisons. That sum equals n * (n - 1) / 2, which grows like n² / 2. Big-O drops the constant factor 1/2 and keeps the shape: doubling `n` roughly quadruples the work.

example.caption: About n * (n - 1) / 2 comparisons in the worst case

sections.heading: Why halving gives log n
sections.body: Halve 1000 again and again: 500, 250, 125, 62, 31, 15, 7, 3, 1. That is about 10 steps, because 2 to the power 10 is 1024. In general, n can be halved about log2(n) times before reaching 1, so doubling the input adds only one more step.
